scenario.speaker: dana
scenario.briefing:
I need a favor — and it's the useful kind of favor, the kind that teaches you something.

The **Wagly** team is behind schedule. Their focus groups are recruited, the facility is booked, and the one thing that doesn't exist yet is the **moderator's guide** — the script the moderator will follow in the room. Marcus assembled a bank of candidate content: openings, icebreakers, discussion questions, and group activities, each with an estimated running time. Your job is to assemble the guide: pick the best option for each part of the introduction, choose one icebreaker, select five discussion questions, and pick two activities.

Two things matter at once: **quality** — neutral, open questions that make people comfortable enough to talk — and **timing**. A well-run ideation group takes about 56 minutes; every choice you make adds its minutes to the session. Watch the running total.

Read my memo and Marcus's checklist in the Inbox first, and skim the Guides. Then build.

inbox.subject: A favor for the Wagly team
inbox.body:
The Wagly focus groups start next week and their moderator's guide doesn't exist yet. I volunteered you. Consider it a compliment.

Here's why I care about this document more than almost any other in qualitative work: **the guide is the study**. A survey can be tightened after a soft launch; a focus group happens once, live, in front of the client. If the guide leads participants, they'll perform agreement instead of giving opinions. If it skips the ground rules, one loud voice will own the room. If it runs long, the moderator will cut the activities — which are usually where the best ideas surface — to make up time.

A guide is not a questionnaire. It's a plan for a *conversation*: it warms people up, earns their trust, moves from their world (their dogs, their routines) toward our world (features, concepts, reactions), and leaves room to probe. Working backward from Wagly's decision: they need **feature ideas and reactions for a second-generation collar**. Everything in the guide should serve that.

Wagly's project brief is attached. Marcus is sending you his checklist separately — he's reviewed more guides than anyone here, so take it seriously. He'll also review what you build.

— Dana

attachments.title: Wagly, Inc. — Focus Group Project Brief
attachments.body:
**Client.** Wagly, Inc. makes a collar-mounted wearable for dogs that tracks health signals (activity, sleep, scratching) and location via GPS. The first-generation collar — about 180,000 active devices — has sold well direct-to-consumer and through specialty pet retailers.

**Business decision.** Wagly is developing a **second-generation product** and must decide which features to build, which to drop, and how owners will react to new directions before engineering budgets are locked.

**Research objectives.**

- Understand how owners currently monitor their dogs' health, activity, and whereabouts — with or without technology
- Surface unmet needs and feature ideas for a next-generation collar, in owners' own words
- Capture reactions to candidate product directions: what appeals, what worries, what's missing
- Identify the improvements owners would prioritize first

**Method.** Four in-person focus groups of 8–10 participants each, professionally moderated, recorded for analysis.

**Participants.** Dog owners, ages 25–65, who are the primary caretaker of at least one dog; mix of current tracking-collar users and non-users in every group.

**Session length.** Approximately one hour per group. The moderator's guide should be built to run in about 56 minutes to leave a margin for late starts and closing logistics.

**Deliverable needed now.** A complete moderator's guide: introduction, icebreaker, discussion questions, and group activities, with timing.

inbox.subject: What separates a great moderator's guide
inbox.body:
Dana says you're building the Wagly guide. Good. Here's the checklist I run every guide through before it leaves the shop:

1. **The introduction sets psychological safety.** Welcome people as people, explain the purpose without naming the client, lay out ground rules that invite disagreement, disclose recording and get consent, and frame the warm-up so nobody feels tested. If participants know who the client is, they start performing for the brand.
2. **The icebreaker is easy and on-topic.** Everyone should be able to answer it without thinking hard, and the answer should point at the subject we're studying — not at trivia.
3. **Questions funnel.** Broad current behavior first, then ideas, then reactions to specific directions. Never start narrow.
4. **Every question opens people up.** No leading, no double-barrels, no yes/no dead-ends, no jargon, and no price hypotheticals before people have even described the product in their own words.
5. **Activities beat interrogation.** One or two structured exercises get quieter participants contributing. But an activity that turns a group into ten people working silently and alone defeats the point of a group.
6. **The math works.** Add up the minutes. If the guide can't run in the booked session, the moderator will improvise cuts — and they'll cut the wrong things.

Build it, and I'll review it against this list.

— Marcus

pages.title: Wagly Moderator's Guide Builder
pages.intro: Assemble Wagly's focus-group moderator's guide. Pick **one option in each part of the introduction**, **one icebreaker**, **five discussion questions**, and **two activities**. Each option shows its estimated running time — the session should total about **56 minutes**.

tasks.title: Create a Moderator's Guide
tasks.prompt: Build the guide section by section. Quality and timing both count: choose neutral, open, well-sequenced content — and keep the running total near the ideal session length.

timeBudget.label: Session length
timeBudget.idealNote: a well-run ideation group takes about 56 minutes

sections.label: Introduction
sections.note: Pick one option for each of the five parts of the introduction.

options.text: "Good evening, everyone — thank you for making time tonight. I'm your moderator. My job is to ask questions, keep us on schedule, and make sure everyone gets heard. I don't work for any product company and nothing you say tonight affects me either way — I'm just here for your honest opinions."

"Welcome! Tonight we're working on behalf of Wagly — the company behind the smart collar some of you may already own. They're a fantastic team with big plans for their next collar, and they're counting on this group for great ideas, so let's make them proud!"

"Tonight we're going to talk about life with your dogs — how you look after their health, activity, and whereabouts, and the products or routines you use to do it. A product team will use what you share to decide what to build next. Your experiences and opinions are the whole point; there are no right or wrong answers."

"Tonight we're going to confirm what we keep hearing everywhere: that dog owners are excited about the next generation of smart collars. We'll spend the hour exploring all the things you love about collar technology and the upgrades you can't wait to buy."

"A few ground rules. One person speaks at a time so the recording is clear. There are no wrong answers — and please disagree with each other; different views are exactly what we're after. I may move us along at times, and that's about the clock, not about your answer. I want to hear from everyone tonight, so I may call on quieter folks. Phones on silent, please."

"Some rules, and I do expect everyone to behave like adults: don't interrupt, don't ramble, don't go off on tangents about your dogs' personalities, and keep every answer short and to the point so we can get through my list on time."

"One important item before we begin: tonight's session is being audio- and video-recorded, and a few members of the research team are observing. The recordings are used only for research analysis; your names are removed from every report, and nothing you say is ever connected to you personally. Is everyone comfortable proceeding on that basis? Please say yes out loud for the recording."
"You might notice cameras around the room — every facility has them, so just ignore them and be yourselves. Let's not burn our hour on housekeeping; we have a lot to get through."

"We'll start easy — just talking about your dogs and your routines — and work our way toward products later in the hour. You are the expert on your own dog and your own household, so speak from your experience. If someone else's story reminds you of something, jump in."
"We have a lot of material and only an hour, so let's skip the small talk and get straight into the product questions — the sooner we start, the sooner we finish."

sections.label: Icebreaker
sections.note: Pick one icebreaker to open the discussion.

options.text: "Let's go around the room: tell us your first name, your dog's name and breed, and what a typical day looks like for the two of you."
"Let's go around the room: tell us your first name and something fun you did last weekend."
"Let's really get to know each other: go around and tell the group about the most embarrassing mistake you've ever made as a pet owner — don't hold back!"

sections.label: Discussion questions
sections.note: Pick five questions. Order matters less than coverage — the moderator will run them broad-to-narrow.

options.text: "Walk me through how you currently keep track of your dog's health, activity, and whereabouts. What do you use — apps, devices, vet visits, plain observation — and when?"
"For those of you who use a tracking collar or pet app today: tell us about a recent time it was genuinely useful — and a time it let you down or made you doubt it."
"Imagine your dog's collar could tell you anything at all about your dog. What would you want it to tell you, and why does that matter to you?"
"I'm going to read a few directions a next-generation collar could take. For each one, tell me what appeals to you, what worries you, and what's missing."
"If the product team could fix or add only one thing in the next version, what should it be — and what makes that the one?"
"How satisfied are you with your collar's battery life and its GPS accuracy?"
"Most owners tell us they'd love automatic vet alerts from their dog's collar. You'd want those too, right?"
"Do you like your dog's current collar?"
"How important are BLE-versus-LTE-M connectivity fallback and geofence polling frequency in your collar purchase decision?"
"If a second-generation collar existed, would you pay $199 for it? Raise your hand for yes."

sections.label: Group activities
sections.note: Pick two activities for the back half of the session.

options.text: Feature card-sort — In pairs, participants sort 15 candidate feature cards (health alerts, GPS fencing, battery options, vet sharing, and more) into three piles: must-have, nice-to-have, and no-thanks, then walk the group through their piles and defend the tough calls aloud.

Draw your ideal collar — Each participant sketches the collar they wish existed for their dog, labeling the parts, then presents the drawing to the group in under a minute. A projective exercise: the drawings surface needs people struggle to put into words.

Individual written questionnaire — Participants put down the discussion and silently complete a 20-item paper questionnaire rating collar features and pricing on their own, without talking to each other, for the remainder of the block.
Brand logo debate — The moderator shows logos from pet-tech brands and participants debate which company has the best logo, name, and packaging, voting on a winner at the end.

guides.title: Anatomy of a Moderator's Guide
guides.body:
A moderator's guide is the script for a focus group — not word-for-word, but a plan the moderator can run under pressure. Nearly every good guide has the same skeleton:

1. **Introduction (~10 min).** Five jobs, in order: a *welcome* that establishes the moderator as a neutral host; a *purpose* statement that explains why everyone is here without revealing the client (once people know the brand, they perform for it); *ground rules* that invite disagreement and share the floor; a *recording disclosure* that tells participants they're being recorded and observed, promises confidentiality, and asks for consent; and a *warm-up framing* that lowers the stakes — no test, no wrong answers, start with their world.
2. **Icebreaker (5–8 min).** One easy question everyone answers. The best icebreakers are low-stakes *and* on-topic: they get every voice in the room early and point the conversation at the subject.
3. **Question funnel (20–30 min).** Broad to narrow. Start with current behavior and experiences (their world), move to needs and ideas, and only then present specific directions for reaction. Starting narrow contaminates everything after it.
4. **Activities (15–20 min).** One or two structured exercises — sorting, ranking, drawing, building. Activities pull contributions from quieter participants and produce artifacts you can analyze later. They belong in the back half, once trust is built.
5. **Close (a few minutes).** Final thoughts, thanks, incentives, dismissal.

**Timing discipline.** Most professional groups are booked for about an hour; a guide that plans **~55–60 minutes of content** leaves margin for late arrivals and long answers. Attention sags past the hour, and recruiters promised participants a specific commitment. Write a minutes number next to every element, add them up, and cut until the total fits. A guide that doesn't fit forces the moderator to improvise cuts live — and the activities, often the most valuable part, are what get cut.

**In this assignment:** every option shows its estimated minutes and the builder shows your running total. The client's brief tells you the session target. Treat the total as part of the deliverable, because it is.

guides.title: Writing Questions That Open People Up
guides.body:
A focus group lives or dies on question wording. The same topic, asked two ways, produces either a conversation or a row of nodding heads. The classic flaws:

- **Leading questions** embed the desired answer. "You'd love a longer battery, right?" tells participants what to say; agreeing is easier than arguing. Fix: ask for experience, not agreement — "Tell me about a time the battery mattered."
- **Double-barreled questions** ask two things at once. "How do you feel about the price and the quality?" gets you an answer to one of them and you won't know which. Fix: one idea per question.
- **Yes/no dead-ends** close the conversation. "Do you like your collar?" earns a "yes" and silence. Fix: start with how, what, walk me through, tell me about.
- **Jargon** makes participants feel tested. Technical or industry terms the client uses internally mean nothing in the room — people either bluff or go quiet. Fix: everyday words, or define the term before asking about it.
- **Premature price hypotheticals.** "Would you pay $X?" asked before people have explored the product produces guesses, not evidence — and the number you name becomes an anchor that skews everything after it. Price talk belongs late, and it should start from the participant's own expectations, not a number you supply.

Two more habits of good discussion questions: they ask about **specific, recent experiences** rather than generalities ("tell me about the last time…"), and they leave the moderator **room to probe** ("what makes that the one?"). If a question can be answered in one word by a bored person, rewrite it.
